contact.primary: The physical touching of two bodies or surfaces; direct interpersonal communication or association.
contact.secondary: In electrical engineering, a conducting part that joins with another to complete or interrupt a circuit.

quotes.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
quotes.quote: True conversation requires intimate **contact** of intellect and generous spiritual communion.

quotes.author: Joseph Conrad
quotes.quote: The ship came into sudden violent **contact** with a submerged derelict beneath the quiet sea.

quotes.author: Michael Faraday
quotes.quote: When the metallic surfaces establish complete **contact**, the voltaic current circulates freely.

intact.primary: Remaining whole, undamaged, or uninjured; complete and unimpaired in all essential parts.
intact.secondary: In biological and anatomical terminology, an organism or structure that has not been altered, dissected, or neutered.

quotes.author: Edward Gibbon
quotes.work: The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
quotes.quote: The ancient monuments of Rome remained almost **intact** until the civil discords of the Middle Ages.

quotes.author: Mary Shelley
quotes.quote: The fragile crystalline ice remained **intact** beneath our feet despite the howling alpine wind.

quotes.author: Charles Darwin
quotes.quote: Many fossil specimens have been preserved perfectly **intact** within deep layers of amber.

intactness.primary: The condition or property of being unbroken, complete, and uninjured; sound integrity.
intactness.secondary: In architectural conservation and historical preservation, maintaining original materials without alteration or loss.

quotes.author: John Ruskin
quotes.quote: The remarkable **intactness** of the ancient mosaic pavement bore witness to Byzantine craftsmanship.

quotes.author: Henry James
quotes.quote: Newman admired the flawless moral **intactness** and dignity of Claire de Cintré's demeanor.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: Dorothea prized the spiritual **intactness** of her convictions above all social convenience.

protactinium.primary: A dense, silvery-gray radioactive metallic chemical element with atomic number 91 and symbol Pa.
protactinium.secondary: In nuclear chemistry and physics, an actinide formed by the decay of uranium-235 and occurring in pitchblende ores.

quotes.author: Marie Curie
quotes.quote: The radioactive decay series of uranium yields intermediate elements including fragile isotopes like **protactinium**.

quotes.author: Ernest Rutherford
quotes.quote: The chemical separation of **protactinium** verified the theoretical disintegration chain of the heavier actinides.

quotes.author: Frederick Soddy
quotes.quote: The parent element of actinium, designated **protactinium**, was isolated through laborious chemical fractionation.

tact.primary: Keen sensitivity in handling difficult individuals or delicate situations; diplomatic finesse and skill.
tact.secondary: In sensory physiology, the sense of touch or cutaneous perception of physical contact.

quotes.author: Jane Austen
quotes.quote: Elizabeth handled Mr. Collins with exquisite **tact**, averting awkward embarrassment in the parlor.

quotes.author: Henry James
quotes.quote: Madame Merle possessed that supreme social **tact** which smooths every rough corner of conversation.

quotes.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
quotes.quote: Genius is common compared to **tact**, which knows how to seize the propitious moment.

tactful.primary: Possessing or displaying a keen sense of what is appropriate, polite, and considerate in dealing with others.
tactful.secondary: Demonstrating diplomatic discretion that avoids causing offense or discomfort in sensitive circumstances.

quotes.author: Edith Wharton
quotes.quote: Newland admired the **tactful** restraint with which Madame Olenska responded to cruel society gossip.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: His **tactful** questions gently elicited her confidence without infringing upon her private sorrow.

quotes.author: Anthony Trollope
quotes.quote: Mr. Arabin offered a **tactful** compromise that soothed the agitated vanity of the archdeacon.

tactfully.primary: In a diplomatic, sensitive, and considerate manner that avoids causing hurt or offense.
tactfully.secondary: With skillful discretion and thoughtful management of delicate human relationships.

quotes.author: Jane Austen
quotes.quote: Mr. Knightley **tactfully** changed the subject when he noticed the painful blush upon Harriet's cheek.

quotes.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
quotes.quote: Watson **tactfully** withdrew to the window, allowing the distressed client to whisper her secret.

quotes.author: Virginia Woolf
quotes.quote: Clarissa steered the dinner conversation **tactfully** past every perilous political disagreement.

tactfulness.primary: The property of possessing delicate discretion and diplomacy in interpersonal interactions.
tactfulness.secondary: Considerate awareness and sensitivity that prevents friction and preserves social harmony.

quotes.author: Henry James
quotes.quote: Strether admired the instinctive **tactfulness** with which Maria Gostrey guided his bewildered steps.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: Philip displayed infinite **tactfulness** in helping Maggie forget her painful family troubles.

quotes.author: Joseph Conrad
quotes.quote: The captain maintained a silent **tactfulness**, shielding the fugitive from the mate's suspicion.

tactic.primary: An action, strategy, or calculated maneuver carefully planned to achieve a specific short-term end.
tactic.secondary: In military science, an individual maneuver executed in the presence of an enemy during battle.

quotes.author: Carl von Clausewitz
quotes.quote: Every tactical maneuver or clever **tactic** must serve the larger strategic objective of the campaign.

quotes.author: Winston Churchill
quotes.quote: The enemy cavalry employed a diversionary **tactic** to draw our vanguard into the rocky defile.

quotes.author: Herman Melville
quotes.quote: The old harpooneer watched the whale's every **tactic**, anticipating its sudden downward plunge.

tactical.primary: Relating to small-scale actions and maneuvers planned to achieve a specific immediate objective.
tactical.secondary: In military doctrine, pertaining to the employment and movement of armed forces in actual combat contact.

quotes.author: Carl von Clausewitz
quotes.quote: The general's supreme **tactical** skill transformed an imminent retreat into an overwhelming victory.

quotes.author: Winston Churchill
quotes.quote: A sound **tactical** deployment along the ridge prevented the gunboats from sustaining severe damage.

quotes.author: Theodore Roosevelt
quotes.quote: Our rapid advance up Kettle Hill demonstrated prompt **tactical** initiative under heavy rifle fire.

tactically.primary: In a calculated manner guided by tactical skill, strategy, and careful maneuvering.
tactically.secondary: With respect to military movements and battlefield deployments in direct combat.

quotes.author: Carl von Clausewitz
quotes.quote: The commander positioned his artillery **tactically** upon the crest to command both river crossings.

quotes.author: Winston Churchill
quotes.quote: The fleet was handled **tactically** with consummate daring throughout the nocturnal engagement.

quotes.author: Theodore Roosevelt
quotes.quote: The frontiersmen were **tactically** superior in dense woodland combat, utilizing every tree for cover.

tactician.primary: An expert in military or political tactics; one skilled in planning and executing strategic maneuvers.
tactician.secondary: A person adept at contriving clever expedients and maneuvers to achieve practical advantages.

quotes.author: Carl von Clausewitz
quotes.quote: Napoleon proved himself the consummate **tactician**, always concentrating superior forces at the decisive point.

quotes.author: Edward Gibbon
quotes.work: The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
quotes.quote: Belisarius was a brilliant **tactician** who compensated for lack of numbers with stratagem and terrain.

quotes.author: Winston Churchill
quotes.quote: As a masterly **tactician**, the Duke anticipated every movement of the opposing French marshals.

tactics.primary: The art and science of disposing military or naval forces in actual combat against an adversary.
tactics.secondary: Calculated methods, devices, or procedures employed to gain a desired objective in politics, business, or sports.

quotes.author: Carl von Clausewitz
quotes.quote: While strategy determines where to fight, **tactics** governs the actual conduct of armed combat.

quotes.author: Sun Tzu
quotes.quote: All men can see the outward **tactics** whereby I conquer, but none can perceive the strategy whence victory is evolved.

quotes.author: Winston Churchill
quotes.quote: New technological weapons demanded revolutionary changes in naval **tactics** and fleet formations.

tactile.primary: Perceptible by touch; tangible; relating to or connected with the sense of touch.
tactile.secondary: In neurophysiology and psychology, mediated by somatosensory receptors in the skin responding to mechanical pressure.

quotes.author: Helen Keller
quotes.quote: Through my fingertips I developed a rich **tactile** sense that opened the great world of literature.

quotes.author: William James
quotes.quote: The **tactile** corpuscles in the fingertips possess extraordinary discriminatory resolution.

quotes.author: John Ruskin
quotes.quote: The sculptor imparts a distinct **tactile** quality to the cold marble, evoking warmth and living flesh.

tactility.primary: The capability of being touched or felt; tangibility; the property of eliciting tactile sensation.
tactility.secondary: In aesthetics and art theory, the felt texture or sculptural dimensionality conveyed by an artistic medium.

quotes.author: Bernard Berenson
quotes.work: The Florentine Painters of the Renaissance
quotes.quote: Giotto rendered figures with astonishing **tactility**, giving two-dimensional frescoes the illusion of solid mass.

quotes.author: William James
quotes.quote: Spatial perception develops through the coordinated interplay of vision and cutaneous **tactility**.

quotes.author: John Ruskin
quotes.quote: The rough-hewn stone surface communicates a rugged **tactility** that smooth stucco can never match.

tactless.primary: Lacking social sensitivity, discretion, or diplomacy; bluntly inconsiderate of others' feelings.
tactless.secondary: Characterized by clumsy words or ill-timed actions that provoke embarrassment or resentment.

quotes.author: Jane Austen
quotes.quote: Mrs. Jennings made many **tactless** inquiries regarding the young lady's matrimonial prospects.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: A single **tactless** remark from the vicar wounded Mr. Casaubon's extraordinarily fragile pride.

quotes.author: Henry James
quotes.quote: Winterbourne regretted his friend's **tactless** laughter, which attracted stares across the hotel terrace.

tactlessly.primary: In an insensitive, blunt, or undiplomatic manner that provokes social embarrassment.
tactlessly.secondary: With clumsy indiscretion and without thoughtful consideration for the feelings of companions.

quotes.author: Jane Austen
quotes.quote: Mrs. Bennet **tactlessly** boasted of Jane's conquests in the presence of the disdainful Darcy.

quotes.author: Edith Wharton
quotes.quote: The gossip blurted out **tactlessly** news that threw the entire gathering into shocked silence.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: He **tactlessly** reminded her of their youthful blunders, opening wounds long thought healed.

tactlessness.primary: The lack of interpersonal sensitivity, discretion, or social diplomacy.
tactlessness.secondary: Clumsy or insensitive behavior that repeatedly causes offense or social discomfort.

quotes.author: Henry James
quotes.quote: The young aristocrat was notorious for the blundering **tactlessness** of his dinner conversation.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: Her mother's persistent **tactlessness** was a source of constant mortification to Gwendolen.

quotes.author: Anthony Trollope
quotes.quote: The squire was exasperated by the unyielding **tactlessness** of his nephew's correspondence.

tactual.primary: Relating to, arising from, or perceived by the sense of touch; tactile.
tactual.secondary: In sensory psychology and neurology, pertaining specifically to somatosensory stimulation and cutaneous contact.

quotes.author: William James
quotes.quote: The brain constructs its spatial map through continuous synthesis of **tactual** and visual impressions.

quotes.author: Helen Keller
quotes.quote: My world is built of **tactual** sensations; my hands are to me what hearing and sight are to others.

quotes.author: Charles Darwin
quotes.work: The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals
quotes.quote: The infant seeks comfort through gentle **tactual** contact with the maternal breast.

tactually.primary: By means of touch; in a manner perceived or verified through physical contact.
tactually.secondary: In experimental psychology, relating to sensations explored and verified through cutaneous contact.

quotes.author: William James
quotes.quote: The blind subject explores the contours of the relief map **tactually** with fine precision.

quotes.author: Helen Keller
quotes.quote: I learned to know the sculpture **tactually**, following every subtle curve of the carved marble.

quotes.author: John Dewey
quotes.quote: A craftsman appreciates material qualities both visually and **tactually** while shaping the timber.

untactful.primary: Lacking tact, sensitivity, or discretion in social interactions; undiplomatic.
untactful.secondary: Displaying an insensitive disregard for the feelings or sensibilities of companions.

quotes.author: Edith Wharton
quotes.quote: The dowager's **untactful** questions brought a momentary flush of indignation to May's cheeks.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: It was an exceedingly **untactful** suggestion to raise before a scholar brooding over unfinished labors.

quotes.author: Anthony Trollope
quotes.quote: His **untactful** intervention in the cabinet debate alienated his staunchest political allies.
